events.excerpt: tl;dr Open-bidding with random deadline (candle auctions) and few auction participants can lead to higher bidder profits than sealed-bid auctions. This is already true in a one-shot auction without explicit coordination or collusion. For the Ethereum builder-market post-Glamsterdam, I conjecture that this gives current participants a strong incentive to maintain the current open-bid auction by restricting outside bidding and per-missioning participation in relay auctions. In this post I want to formalize a piece of folk knowledge which I think is well-known among many searchers, builders and other participants of the MEV ecosystem: Open bidding auctions with a random deadline and few participants tend to give those participants more payoff than a sealed auction. On a high level, the logic is straightforward. Uncertainty about the auction deadline (in the case of PoS Ethereum through heterogeneous proposer behavior (timing games) and locations) creates for equally fast bidders with equal value a quasi-lottery: Bidders can outbid each other in small increments and whoever manages to place the last bid before the auction ends wins. This is preferable for them to bidding their full value away in a sealed auction (with certain deadline). The idea dates back to Ethereum PoW times where
events.headline: Why searchers and builders like candle auctions (and why it matters for the builder market post-Glamsterdam)

events.excerpt: Summary Rollups scaled by moving execution off the L1, but the authentication part of every transaction still goes to the L1. That makes data the likely bottleneck for L2 scaling in the PQ era, even with more blobs. PQ signatures are far larger than ECDSA, so if every L2 user switched to one, signatures would make up 99% of transaction data and the transfers that fit in 6 blobs would fall from about 6,600 to 155. ZK applications have it worse, since a single PQ proof usually does not fit in 3 blobs. Either way, the bottleneck is that the cost of checking trust grows with the number of users. An L2 can cut this cost by adopting EIP-8288: signatures and proofs move out of transactions, and the statements of many blocks are bundled into one leanVM aggregate proof posted to the L1. A transaction authenticated with leanSPHINCS then compresses to 100 to 129 bytes, close to an ECDSA transaction. A 32-core machine (AWS c7a.8xlarge) can prove up to 170 leanSPHINCS signatures per second on a 2-second chain. At that load, the 2,040 leanSPHINCS transactions arriving per L1 block fit in 2.8 to 3.3 blobs on average, calculated from the measured aggregate size and compression ratio. Without EIP-8288 aggregates, carrying the signatures in the transactions would take 79 blobs for the same transac
events.headline: It's time to scale the trust: EIP-8288 on OP Stack

events.excerpt: Most key-compromise defenses today (smart wallets, ERC-7579 modules, social recovery, EIP-7702 delegation) enforce policy in the account’s code. ERC-8403 continues this: spend limits and unlock times are authorities committed under the account’s root. I’d like to probe a different placement: enforcing rate limits at the asset : the token contract for ERC-20s, and eventually the protocol itself for native ETH. Motivation. Account-level policy only binds while the account’s code is in the transfer path. Two gaps: Allowances : a contract holding an existing transferFrom approval moves tokens without re-entering the wallet’s validation logic, so a wallet-level daily limit does not bind. Delegation replacement : under EIP-7702, the compromised EOA key can re-delegate and strip the policy that was supposed to contain it. An asset-level check binds every balance-reducing path ( transfer , transferFrom , burns) regardless of which application initiated it, and survives delegation changes. Sketch (details negotiable, that is the point of the thread): Optional per-account spending limit (rolling window) enforced where balances change. Security-weakening changes (raising or removing a limit, replacing a recovery address) take effect after a delay of about 14 days; security-strengthening cha
events.headline: Asset-level spending limits and recovery: should rate limiting live in the asset rather than the account?

events.excerpt: Abstract PropAMMs are on-chain venues whose prices are set by a single maker. The maker pushes quote state on-chain, and fills read that state. We decoded 92,627 fills on nine Ethereum PropAMMs over 30 days (10 September to 9 October 2026) from execution data. We priced the 69,827 WETH/stablecoin fills against Binance one-second trades. Three of the registry venues accept maker state only if it is stamped with the current block’s timestamp. Their fills always execute against an update in the same block. Takers pay about 0.45 bp at the fill, on every one of the 30 days. Over the following five minutes the price does not move in their favour on average, in any taker class: there is no sign of adverse selection. Of fills after a CEX move of more than 0.5 bp in the preceding 12 seconds, 78.5% trade against it. The PropAMM quote follows the CEX in the same block, while Uniswap lags. Arbitrage contracts and routers use the PropAMM as the fresh side of a trade against a stale AMM. Fills are priced no later than their block’s sealing, which relays received 0.1 to 3.1 s after the slot start on the two days measured. Markouts change by under 0.1 bp across that range. events.headline: PropAMM fills on Ethereum mainnet and PropAMM support for TEMBRI (toolbox): same-block quotes, a small spread, and flow taken from lagging AMMs

events.excerpt: ⚠️ Security: CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel) CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack. It is not specific to MPTCP, but the demonstrated remote exploit requires an MPTCP listener, which Go 1.24+ enables by default. This release disables MPTCP listeners in lnd by default , which closes the demonstrated exploit path through lnd. It is a mitigation, not a fix: the kernel patch is the only fix. Linux operators should: Upgrade to this release. Disable MPTCP on the host ( sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0 ), since other services on the machine are not covered by this release. Install a patched kernel as soon as your distribution ships one. If you cannot upgrade yet, start your existing binary with the environment variable GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 , which turns off Go's default MPTCP listeners. Do not set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=1 to re-enable MPTCP until your kernel is patched. The Go team's discussion of the issue is at golang/go#82717 . See the release notes for the full instructions, including Docker and firewall guidance. Windows and macOS are not affected. Database Migrations There are no migrations in this release. It turns simulation from a trusted frontend service into a reproducible, machine-checkable artifact that can be bound into signatures and Scoped Capability Tokens. Enables “recompute on a component the UI does not control.” Motivation: A simulation served by a compromised frontend is worthless. Independence + canonicity closes the UI/calldata mismatch class of attacks. events.excerpt: On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems. Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar , TÜRKTRUST , and TrustWave ), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independentl
events.headline: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys

events.excerpt: A Kusama Wish for Change needs a 666.67 KSM decision deposit before it can go to a vote. Governance takes that deposit from one account. A proposal can have support and still time out because nobody can carry the whole amount. We have built a contract that lets people and groups share it. The first pool is live for our Wish for Change #676 . We are asking for code review and people to try the Paseo rehearsal. This is experimental and has not had an independent review. We deployed before that review to leave time before #676 times out. A killed referendum loses the deposit, and a contract bug could also put contributions at risk. Kusama pool : real KSM. Paseo rehearsal : free test PAS. Source, tests and logs . Verified Kusama contract . How it works Each pool is fixed to one referendum and its exact deposit. It has no owner, admin key or upgrade path. People contribute from their own accounts. The payment that fills the pool tries to place the deposit in the same transaction. If placement fails, the contribution stays in the pool and anyone can retry. Contributors can withdraw while the pool remains open, before placement. After the referendum ends, anyone can reclaim the deposit and send payouts to the contributing accounts. These are separate contract calls. No watcher is runnin
events.headline: Collaborative decision deposits: live on Kusama, open for review

events.excerpt: This story is interesting: One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about. Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go. It’s interesting because it exposes all the insecurities in this piece of IoT software. But I think the real story is that a random person was able to do this reverse-engineering with the help of AI. Expect a lot more stories like this in the future.
events.headline: Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts

events.excerpt: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. events.excerpt: Digital signatures control who can spend funds, issue commands and authorize requests. Widely used schemes rely on factoring or discrete logarithms, assumptions threatened by Shor’s quantum algorithm. The post-quantum transition therefore reaches the mechanism used to establish authority itself. Post-quantum signatures provide replacements with different security assumptions, key sizes, signature sizes and verification costs. Applications that also prove execution must express that verification in their proof arithmetic. Signatureless authorization takes a direct proof-of-knowledge approach. An authority publishes a commitment to a reusable secret. Each action is authorized by a freshly randomized zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of that secret, bound to the requested action. The central security problem is safe reuse: an adversary can collect valid proofs, adapt later requests to earlier responses and attempt to authorize a fresh request. The linked paper develops this construction and proves a quantum chosen-request security reduction in an explicit address-compatible random-completion model. It also establishes the bindings for recursive verification. Parano1d supplies the implementation and measurements. The interface supports both standalone requests and authorization compo
events.headline: Post-quantum signatureless authorization with recursive verification

events.excerpt: Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One , Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network . Key insights Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure. Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods.
